prompt.context: Your client is a large hospital chain, K. Grace. There have been proposed legislation changes to Medicare that will affect your client. For example, some surgeries will no longer be reimbursable at the same rate. As a result, this has caused the hospital to consider a strategy that would shift its focus toward less profitable surgeries by using alternative therapies. However, the client is concerned about the decreased revenue potential from this proposed shift in strategy. Currently the client has a $4 billion top line. Surgeries represent half of this total. Half of the hospitals in the chain perform all of these surgeries. For this case, let's say that all patients are on Medicare (private insurance is not a factor).
prompt.question: Should we close part of the chain? All of the chain? None of the chain? What drivers will help us arrive at a close / no close decision?

clarifying_info.q: What are the typical financials for an impacted hospital?
clarifying_info.a: Each hospital sees 1,000 patients per year. Revenue per patient is $1,000. Cost per patient is $800. Fixed cost of the facility is $100,000 per year.

clarifying_info.q: What does it cost to exit / close a hospital?
What is K. Grace's national market share?
clarifying_info.a: The client holds a 20% national market share.

framework: Profitability analysis: break down revenues (price x quantity) and costs (fixed vs. variable) for impacted hospitals
Breakeven analysis: determine minimum patient volume required to keep a facility open
Exit cost analysis: compare PV of future losses against the one-time cost of closure
Strategic alternatives: assess whether the hospital chain can enter the alternative therapy market
External / regulatory environment: evaluate ability to influence legislation; assess whether patients would pay out-of-pocket
Competitive landscape: understand strategies being adopted by competing hospital chains

questions.prompt: Part I — Basic breakeven: Using the given unit economics, at what patient volume does a typical impacted hospital break even?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify contribution margin per patient ($1,000 - $800 = $200) and divide fixed costs by that margin. Should also note that the break-even volume is 500 patients.

math.setup: Contribution margin per patient = Revenue per patient - Variable cost per patient = $1,000 - $800 = $200. Break-even: Fixed Costs / Contribution Margin = patients needed.

questions.prompt: Part II — Close decision: How many patients would the hospital have to lose below the break-even of 500 to justify closure, given an exit cost of $50,000?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that closing only makes sense when the PV of future losses equals the exit cost. Use a perpetuity framework: annual loss / discount rate = exit cost. Assume a 10% discount rate.

math.setup: Annual loss / discount rate = exit cost. Annual loss = number of patients below breakeven x $200 contribution margin. Solve for the number of patients below 500 that makes closure worthwhile.
steps: Minimum patients to remain open = 500 - 25 = 475 patients
math.answer: If the hospital drops below 475 patients, it should close. The hospital must lose at least 25 patients below the 500 break-even point.

questions.prompt: Part III — Sensitivity: If fixed costs increase to $150,000, what is the new break-even? How many patients below the new break-even would justify closure?
questions.guidance: Candidate repeats the same logic with new fixed costs. New break-even rises to 750. The closure threshold (25 patients below break-even) is unchanged because the exit cost and discount rate are the same.

math.setup: New break-even = $150,000 / $200. Closure threshold calculation unchanged: loss / 0.10 = $50,000.
steps: Patients below new break-even to justify closure = $5,000 / $200 = 25 patients
Minimum patients to remain open = 750 - 25 = 725 patients
math.answer: New break-even is 750 patients. Hospital should close if it falls below 725 patients.

questions.prompt: Part IV — Contradiction check: The hospital finds that 3/8 of its surgeries will not be reimbursable. A government report says the new legislation will save 6-9%. You know someone has botched the research. How is the information contradictory?
questions.guidance: Candidate must ask for the client's national market share to make the comparison meaningful. With a 20% national share, the client's impacted surgeries represent 3/8 x 20% = 7.5% of national spending. This is within the 6-9% government savings range, so the numbers are not necessarily contradictory from the government's perspective — but the candidate should flag that comparing a firm-level fraction (3/8 of client surgeries) directly to a national savings percentage (6-9%) is an apples-to-oranges comparison without knowing market share.

math.setup: Client's share of national surgery market = client market share x fraction of client surgeries impacted.
steps: Client's contribution to national savings = 37.5% x 20% = 7.5%
math.answer: 7.5% of national savings comes from K. Grace's impacted surgeries. This is within the government's stated 6-9% range, so the internal research figure of 3/8 appears to over-state the impact relative to the national figure unless the market share assumption is clarified. The data is contradictory because comparing a firm-level surgery fraction to a national savings percentage without adjusting for market share is an invalid comparison.

brainstorming.prompt: What capabilities or market opportunities might allow K. Grace to offset lost surgical revenue through alternative therapies?

categories.name: Internal capabilities
ideas: Existing clinical staff who could be retrained for alternative therapy delivery
Physical space that could be repurposed for outpatient alternative therapy clinics
Brand and patient trust that could transfer to new service lines

categories.name: Market demand
ideas: Patient willingness to pay out-of-pocket for alternative therapies not covered by Medicare
Aging population trends increasing demand for non-surgical pain management
Employer health plans that may reimburse alternative therapies

categories.name: Competitive positioning
ideas: First-mover advantage in alternative therapy if competitors are slow to pivot
Partnership with specialized alternative therapy providers
Acquisition of existing alternative therapy clinic networks

recommendation: Conduct a hospital-by-hospital profitability review to identify which facilities fall below or near the 475-patient threshold (or 725 if fixed costs rise to $150,000) and prioritize closure of those units
Do not close the entire chain; profitable facilities above breakeven should continue operating, as the legislation change does not affect all revenue
Explore entry into alternative therapies as a revenue offset, contingent on demonstrating sufficient patient demand and reimbursement potential
risks: Patient volume projections may be uncertain; actual post-legislation volumes could be higher or lower than modeled
Exit costs may be underestimated (e.g., labor contracts, facility remediation, reputational effects)
Alternative therapy market may not generate margins comparable to surgery; cannibalizes brand positioning
Regulatory environment could shift again, making closures difficult to reverse
next_steps: Gather patient-volume forecasts by facility under the new Medicare rules
Model full exit costs (legal, severance, lease) for candidate closure facilities
Assess competitive response and benchmark alternative therapy margins
Engage regulatory/government affairs team to understand influence options on the proposed legislation
